title: Звонок Елены и паника поваров  (Elena's Call and the Cooks' Panic)

segments.t: Elena Pavlovna calls Viktor Petrovich to thank him for the wonderful surprise dish and agrees to meet him in an hour. Meanwhile, the cooks realize that Chef Barinov tasted the fugu fish himself and begins feeling numb, sparking full-blown panic in the kitchen.
Тогда что же, встретимся через час?
А что, там холодно, быстрее отойдет?
Now let's go back through the conversation line by line.

'Elena Pavlovna, forgive me, my...' Barinov gently voices this formal apology while facing Elena using "prostite" ("forgive me") — a warmer, more earnest polite apology that literally asks someone to forgive you.
'Believe me, it was absolutely delightful.' Vika fires back promptly in front of Barinov and brings in "voskhititelnym" ("delightful", from "voskhititelnyy") as the key Russian word here.

'I am glad that you liked it.' Insisting on how glad she is in front of Vika, the "-sya" ending on "ponravilos" ("pleased, was liked") marks an action that unfolds mutually or turns back on the speaker.
'I thank you.' Barinov casually directs this polite thanks as they meet using "blagodaryu" ("I thank you") — literally "I give thanks", a slightly more formal way to say thank you than "spasibo".
'It is nothing, nothing at all, do not worry.' Vika opens up dryly on the spot and centers the thought on "perezhivayte" ("worry", from "perezhivat") without wasting a word.
'Excuse me. It is nothing.' Elena casually gives this polite apology as they meet using "izvinite" ("excuse me") — the respectful form of "excuse me" or "sorry" used when stepping in or apologizing.
'Everything is fine.' Barinov opens up warmly without any doubt, grounding the moment in plain reality.
'Hello, Viktor Petrovich.' Leaning in briskly before Barinov, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 3 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
Тогда что же, встретимся через час?

'Then what do you say we meet in an hour?' Dwelling on an hour in front of Barinov, the "-sya" ending on "vstretimsya" ("we'll meet") marks an action that unfolds mutually or turns back on the speaker.
'I will be driving my car.' Barinov speaks quietly in their talk, watching Elena's face to see how the news lands.
'We have to stop him.' Vika cuts in readily beside Barinov and reaches for the Russian word "ostanovit" ("to stop") right at the heart of the line.
'It makes no difference now.' Weighing in quietly in the exchange, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 3 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
А что, там холодно, быстрее отойдет?
'What, since it is cold in there, will it wear off faster?' Barinov quizzes wryly whether Elena really thought this through.
Тогда что же, встретимся через час?
А что, там холодно, быстрее отойдет?

That wraps up this scene as elena calls Viktor Petrovich to thank him for the delicious dish and arrange a meeting in an hour, while the cooks panic after realizing the Chef tasted the fugu himself. Until next time!
